stories.headline: Magnitude 7.7 earthquake moved the ground by up to 1.2 m on Panama's Azuero peninsula
stories.subtitle: Magnitude 7.7 earthquake, 9 October 2026
stories.metricLabel: Ground motion along the satellite's line of sight
stories.confidenceNote: One interferogram from two passes. Motion is along the satellite's line of sight only; atmosphere and unwrapping errors can affect it
stories.summary: Two radar passes 12 days apart, on 2 October 2026 and 14 October 2026, bracket the 9 October 2026 earthquake. Comparing them shows the ground moved by up to 1.2 m along the satellite's line of sight. Across the map the two extremes differ by about 1.4 m, which is 11 colour cycles ('fringes') of 12 cm each. On the map, the darker the green, the more the ground moved.
causes: Sudden slip on the fault that ruptured in the magnitude 7.7 earthquake (USGS: 9 October 2026, about 10 km deep)
The magnitude 6.6, 6.0 and 6.1 aftershocks, which all fall inside the same 12-day window and add to the total
A small part of any radar interferogram is atmosphere (water vapour) or ionosphere, not ground motion
stories.whyItMatters: Radar fringes show where and how far the ground moved, including places no seismometer or GPS station reaches. That helps responders and engineers see which parts of the peninsula were shaken and shifted most.
stories.nextStep: Compare with GPS stations, field reports and a second NISAR pair from a different track before using the numbers for damage or fault models.
stories.explanation:
NASA-ISRO NISAR flew over the Azuero peninsula on 2 October 2026 and again on 14 October 2026, from the same track and look direction. The earthquake (magnitude 7.7, 9 October 2026, 10 km deep, per USGS) happened in between, with aftershocks of M6.6 on 9 October (20:25 UTC), M6.0 on 10 October, M6.1 on 12 October.

An interferogram compares the radar phase of the two passes. If the ground has not moved, the phase matches. If it moved even a few centimetres towards or away from the satellite, the phase shifts: one full colour cycle means the distance changed by half the L-band wavelength, about 12 cm. Counting cycles across the map gives about 11 fringes: the 1st to 99th percentile of the map runs from -1.16 m to +0.22 m, so the two extremes are about 1.4 m apart and the largest motion in either direction is 1.2 m.

The map is zeroed in the far field (median of 176001 far-field pixels), because an unwrapped phase only gives relative motion. Pixels with coherence below 0.3 are left out (the average coherence of what is shown is 0.54), so the map covers about 3,638 km2 rather than the whole frame.

What this does not say: radar sees motion along one slanted line, not up, east and north separately, so 'up to 1.2 m' is not the full 3D movement. Atmosphere, the ionosphere and unwrapping errors where coherence is low can add or remove fringes. The aftershocks fall inside the same 12 days, so this is the sum of all of them.

Why it matters: Radar fringes show where and how far the ground moved, including places no seismometer or GPS station reaches. That helps responders and engineers see which parts of the peninsula were shaken and shifted most. Compare with GPS stations, field reports and a second NISAR pair from a different track before using the numbers for damage or fault models.
paragraphs: A magnitude 7.7 earthquake struck here on 9 Oct 2026. NISAR flew over twice, on 2 Oct and 14 Oct, so the two passes sit either side of the shock.
Putting them together shows the ground moved by up to 1.2 m along the satellite's line of sight. Across the map the two extremes are about 1.4 m apart.

That is a lot. Radar can pick up movements of a few centimetres: each of the 11 colour cycles on the picture is only about 12 cm, so a metre or more is large. The picture covers about 3,638 km² around the earthquake, measured from space.
Aftershocks of magnitude 6.6, 6.0 and 6.1 fell in the same 12 days, so the map shows all of them together.
stories.metricLine: Up to 1.2 m of ground motion · 2 Oct – 14 Oct 2026

stories.headline: Open water is spreading across the Everglades
stories.subtitle: Freshwater marsh and sawgrass prairie
stories.confidenceNote: Exploratory dB thresholds on L-band backscatter, not a validated flood map
stories.summary: Radar measured 12.5% of the analysed area as open water on 15 October 2026. That is more than the 4.2% measured on 17 June 2026. Open water looks dark to radar: a smooth surface reflects the signal away from the satellite instead of back to it.
causes: Seasonal rainfall refilling ponds and sloughs after the 2026 drought
Water managed through canals and control structures
Vegetation burned in the August 2026 fire, exposing open water
stories.whyItMatters: The Everglades depends on slow, shallow sheet flow. Summer 2026 brought extreme drought and then fire in peat soil, so how much of the marsh is wet again decides what wildlife, fire risk and Florida's water supply look like next.
stories.nextStep: Compare with water-level gauges from the South Florida Water Management District and optical imagery before treating the change as confirmed.
stories.explanation:
NISAR passed over the Everglades 10 times between 17 June 2026 and 15 October 2026, all from the same track and look direction so the measurements can be compared. Each pass records two polarisations, HH and HV. Open water looks dark to radar: a smooth surface reflects the signal away from the satellite instead of back to it. Pixels darker than -15 dB in HH and -22 dB in HV are counted as open water.

Across those passes the share of the analysed area classed as open water grew from 4.2% to 12.5%, a change of +8.3 percentage points. The lowest reading was 4.1% on 28 August 2026 and the highest 27.0% on 3 October 2026, a trend of about +5.0 percentage points per month. The outline on the map is every part of the area that was open water in at least one month, and it covers about 390 km².

What this does not say: these are threshold rules on radar brightness, not a verified flood map. Wind roughening the water surface, wet soil after rain and a different look angle can all move the same numbers. Short, sharp changes between two passes are more likely to be weather or geometry than real change on the ground.

Why it matters: The Everglades depends on slow, shallow sheet flow. Summer 2026 brought extreme drought and then fire in peat soil, so how much of the marsh is wet again decides what wildlife, fire risk and Florida's water supply look like next. Compare with water-level gauges from the South Florida Water Management District and optical imagery before treating the change as confirmed.
paragraphs: More of this area is under open water. It grew from 4.2% of the area on 17 Jun to 12.5% on 15 Oct.
It peaked at 27.0% on 3 Oct, about 6 times the 17 Jun level, then fell back to 12.5%.
The biggest single change came between 28 Aug and 9 Sep, when it went from 4.1% to 23.3%.
NISAR looked 10 times from the same angle, so the passes can be compared. Calm water is smooth, so it bounces the radar signal away and shows up dark.
stories.metricLine: 12.5 % of area under open water · 17 Jun – 15 Oct 2026

stories.subtitle: Freshwater marsh and sawgrass prairie
stories.confidenceNote: Exploratory dB thresholds on L-band backscatter, not a validated flood map
stories.summary: Radar measured 8.4% of the analysed area as flooded vegetation on 15 October 2026. That is more than the 4.4% measured on 17 June 2026. Flooded vegetation looks very bright to radar: water and plant stems form a corner that bounces the signal straight back, while the cross-polarised signal stays weak.
causes: Rain-fed water rising into sawgrass and other marsh vegetation
Wet-season sheet flow spreading slowly across the marsh
Marsh plants regrowing through standing water after the fire

The outline on the map is every part of the area that was flooded vegetation in at least one month, and it covers about 73 km².

Wind roughening the water surface, wet soil after rain and a different look angle can all move the same numbers. Short, sharp changes between two passes are more likely to be weather or geometry than real change on the ground.

Summer 2026 brought extreme drought and then fire in peat soil, so how much of the marsh is wet again decides what wildlife, fire risk and Florida's water supply look like next. Compare with water-level gauges from the South Florida Water Management District and optical imagery before treating the change as confirmed.
paragraphs: More of the marsh here is flooded under the plants. It grew from 4.4% of the area on 17 Jun to 8.4% on 15 Oct.
It peaked at 10.4% on 11 Jul, about 2 times the 17 Jun level, then fell back to 8.4%.
The biggest single change came between 29 Jun and 11 Jul, when it went from 4.8% to 10.4%.

NISAR looked 10 times from the same angle, so the passes can be compared. Water standing among plants makes a corner that sends the signal straight back, so it shows up very bright. A normal camera from space cannot see water hidden under plants.

causes: The annual flood pulse arriving from the Angolan highlands
Seasonal evaporation drawing channels down
stories.whyItMatters: The Okavango's flood pulse decides where wildlife, cattle and people find water each year.
stories.nextStep: Compare with river gauge records upstream before treating the change as confirmed.

Pixels darker than -15 dB in HH and -22 dB in HV are counted as open water.

The lowest reading was 14.3% on 12 October 2026 and the highest 51.1% on 8 July 2026, a trend of about -10.5 percentage points per month. The outline on the map is every part of the area that was open water in at least one month, and it covers about 802 km².

What this does not say: these are threshold rules on radar brightness, not a verified flood map. Wind roughening the water surface, wet soil after rain and a different look angle can all move the same numbers. Short, sharp changes between two passes are more likely to be weather or geometry than real change on the ground.

Why it matters: The Okavango's flood pulse decides where wildlife, cattle and people find water each year. Compare with river gauge records upstream before treating the change as confirmed.
paragraphs: Less of this area is under open water. It fell from 48.0% of the area on 26 Jun to 14.3% on 12 Oct.
Only about 30% of the 26 Jun amount is left.
The biggest single change came between 8 Jul and 20 Jul, when it went from 51.1% to 42.5%.

causes: Water rising into standing reeds and marsh vegetation
Seasonal flooding of fish farms and marsh margins
Vegetation growing up through shallow standing water
stories.whyItMatters: Lake Manzala is one of Egypt's largest coastal wetlands. How much of it is open water and how much is flooded marsh decides what fishing, farming and wildlife it can support.

The lowest reading was 2.3% on 8 July 2026 and the highest 3.4% on 18 September 2026, a trend of about +0.2 percentage points per month. The readings moved between 2.3% and 3.4% from pass to pass, so this net change is small and easy to mistake for normal wobble.

stories.headline: Radar maps a burn scar of about 31 km² in Big Sur
stories.subtitle: Plaskett Fire · Los Padres National Forest
stories.confidenceNote: Exploratory thresholds on the drop in L-band cross-polarised radar, not a validated burn map
stories.summary: Comparing NISAR's radar pass on 3 October 2026 with 16 August 2026, before the fire, about 31 km² lost so much cross-polarised signal that it is likely burned, and another 15 km² is possibly burned. Healthy vegetation returns a strong cross-polarised (HV) radar signal from the leaves and branches of forest and chaparral; when fire removes them, the signal drops by several decibels.
causes: Fire burning through forest and chaparral canopy, removing leaves and branches
Severe burns on steep slopes leaving bare soil and standing dead trunks
Smaller drops can also come from drying vegetation or a change in soil moisture
stories.whyItMatters: Burned slopes above Highway 1 are prone to debris flows and landslides once the winter rains arrive. Knowing where the canopy is gone helps decide which roads, creeks and communities need protection first.
stories.nextStep: Compare with the official fire perimeter, Sentinel-2 burn-severity (dNBR) maps and NASA FIRMS hotspots before treating the outline as the burn scar.
stories.explanation:
NISAR passed over Big Sur 6 times between 16 August 2026 and 15 October 2026, all from the same track and look direction so the passes can be compared. Each pass was compared with 16 August 2026, the last pass before the fire started. Healthy vegetation returns a strong cross-polarised (HV) radar signal from the leaves and branches of forest and chaparral; when fire removes them, the signal drops by several decibels. Before comparing, the radar brightness was averaged over about 100 m to reduce speckle. Pixels whose HV fell by more than 3 dB are counted as likely burned, and by 2–3 dB as possibly burned.

While the fire was burning, the likely-burned area read 0.3 km² on 28 August 2026, 19 km² on 9 September 2026 and 25 km² on 21 September 2026. On 3 October 2026, the first pass after the fire period, it was 31 km², with 15 km² more possibly burned. The last pass, on 15 October 2026, read 41 km², so the area kept growing after the fire period. That can mean the fire was still spreading at its edges, or that scorched vegetation kept drying out and losing its leaves. On the map, the burned patches are filled in two colours, likely and possibly burned; together they cover about 46 km². The story outline is drawn around them.

Fire reports put the fire at about 121 km² (29,862 acres on 8 September 2026, 47% contained). The radar's likely-burned area is 26% of that, and 38% with the possibly burned pixels added. A reported fire area is the whole perimeter: it includes unburned islands and ground fire under a canopy that survived, where the radar signal barely changes, so the radar is expected to flag less than the reported area. Source: https://bigsurkate.blog/2026/09/08/.

What this does not say: these are threshold rules on radar brightness, not a verified burn-severity map. Drying vegetation, a change in soil moisture after rain and wind in the vegetation can also lower the signal. Steep slopes facing away from the satellite are poorly seen, and the fire may have burned there too. Treat the outline as where to look first, not as the official burn scar.

Why it matters: Burned slopes above Highway 1 are prone to debris flows and landslides once the winter rains arrive. Knowing where the canopy is gone helps decide which roads, creeks and communities need protection first. Compare with the official fire perimeter, Sentinel-2 burn-severity (dNBR) maps and NASA FIRMS hotspots before treating the outline as the burn scar.
paragraphs: A fire burned part of this area. Radar picked up about 31.3 km² of ground that is likely burned, and another 15 km² that is possibly burned, compared with 16 Aug, before the fire.
The burned area kept growing: 40.5 km² by 15 Oct.
Fire strips the leaves and branches that bounce part of the radar signal back, so burned ground goes dark. Radar sees through smoke and cloud, day or night, which a normal camera from space cannot.

stories.headline: Radar maps a burn scar of about 19 km² in Everglades National Park
stories.subtitle: Drought fires in the sawgrass marshes · Florida
stories.confidenceNote: Exploratory thresholds on the drop in L-band cross-polarised radar, not a validated burn map
stories.summary: Comparing NISAR's radar pass on 25 August 2026 with 20 July 2026, before the fire, about 19 km² lost so much cross-polarised signal that it is likely burned, and another 30 km² is possibly burned. Healthy vegetation returns a strong cross-polarised (HV) radar signal from the leaves and stems of sawgrass and other marsh plants; when fire removes them, the signal drops by several decibels.
causes: Fire burning through drought-dried sawgrass and marsh vegetation
Ground fire in exposed peat soils, which can smoulder after the flames pass
Smaller drops can also come from vegetation dying back in the drought, or from water returning to the marsh after rain
stories.whyItMatters: Burned sawgrass usually regrows, but when drought lets fire reach the peat, it burns away soil that took centuries to build, releases stored carbon and changes how water flows through the River of Grass.
stories.nextStep: Compare with the park's fire perimeters, Sentinel-2 burn-severity (dNBR) maps and NASA FIRMS hotspots, and check water levels, before treating the outline as the burn scar.
stories.explanation:
NISAR passed over Everglades National Park 6 times between 20 July 2026 and 30 September 2026, all from the same track and look direction so the passes can be compared. Each pass was compared with 20 July 2026, the last pass before the fire started. Healthy vegetation returns a strong cross-polarised (HV) radar signal from the leaves and stems of sawgrass and other marsh plants; when fire removes them, the signal drops by several decibels. Before comparing, the radar brightness was averaged over about 100 m to reduce speckle. Pixels whose HV fell by more than 3 dB are counted as likely burned, and by 2–3 dB as possibly burned.

While the fire was burning, the likely-burned area read 39 km² on 13 August 2026. On 25 August 2026, the first pass after the fire period, it was 19 km², with 30 km² more possibly burned. The last pass, on 30 September 2026, read 411 km², so the area kept growing after the fire period. That can mean the fire was still spreading at its edges, or that scorched vegetation kept drying out and losing its leaves. On the map, the burned patches are filled in two colours, likely and possibly burned; together they cover about 41 km². The story outline is drawn around them.

Fire reports put the fire at about 97 km² (nearly 24,000 acres across four fires in the park, 26 August 2026). The radar's likely-burned area is 19% of that, and 51% with the possibly burned pixels added. A reported fire area is the whole perimeter: it includes unburned islands and ground fire under a canopy that survived, where the radar signal barely changes, so the radar is expected to flag less than the reported area. Source: https://www.wlrn.org/environment/2026-08-26/drought-fire-everglades-peat-national-park.

What this does not say: these are threshold rules on radar brightness, not a verified burn-severity map. Drying vegetation, a change in soil moisture after rain and wind in the vegetation can also lower the signal. In a wetland, standing water returning after rain darkens the radar much as a burn does, so drops in later passes may be water rather than fire. Treat the outline as where to look first, not as the official burn scar.

Why it matters: Burned sawgrass usually regrows, but when drought lets fire reach the peat, it burns away soil that took centuries to build, releases stored carbon and changes how water flows through the River of Grass. Compare with the park's fire perimeters, Sentinel-2 burn-severity (dNBR) maps and NASA FIRMS hotspots, and check water levels, before treating the outline as the burn scar.
paragraphs: A fire burned part of this area. Radar picked up about 18.8 km² of ground that is likely burned, and another 30 km² that is possibly burned, compared with 20 Jul, before the fire.
Later passes read much higher, up to 538 km² on 18 Sep. Rain and wet soil can also darken the radar signal, so 18.8 km² is the careful figure.
Fire strips the leaves and branches that bounce part of the radar signal back, so burned ground goes dark. Radar sees through smoke and cloud, day or night, which a normal camera from space cannot.
